attribution.note: Marcus wrote this on his own Substack. He includes himself in 'All of us expect', so he endorses the expectation.

semantics.note: 'Expect' is an unqualified expectation of a definite outcome, so this is a scored forecast. The normalised proposition matches the statement, which gives no deadline or metric.

contract.note: The plain reading (AI substantially changes everyday programming work) is an ordinary reading of 'big impact on coding'. It does not require productivity or job effects. The five-year horizon comes from the panel's framing, not from Marcus's sentence. That is a reasonable outer bound.

evidence.note: Stack Overflow 2026 survey, published 2026-10-06, before the evaluation date. Coding assistants and agents are the top AI use case, with heavy daily use. The headline 73% applies to users of these tools, not to all developers.

Same survey, with the denominator clarified: 73% of coding-assistant users use them daily. Main tasks are generating familiar code and debugging, which is actual workflow use rather than planned adoption.
METR says productivity effects are poorly measured because of selection effects. Developers declining to work without AI points to deep integration. It does not bear on the workflow reading.

reviews.rationale: The contextual deadline is 2031, but the contract's early-resolution rule is met. A dated, broad international developer survey (Stack Overflow, Oct 2026) documents routine daily use of AI for core coding tasks such as code generation and debugging at substantial scale. METR's caveats are about measuring productivity, not about workflow change, so they do not contradict the claim under the workflow reading.

attribution.note: Marcus wrote on his own Substack that he is on the 'large impact' side for education, which endorses the view.

semantics.note: Placing himself on the 'large impact' side is an unhedged expectation, so this is a scored forecast. The words of caution qualify the view but are not an antecedent that must occur. No deadline or metric is given.

contract.note: Reading the claim as substantial, widespread change to teaching, learning or assessment, good or bad, is ordinary and fair. The five-year horizon to Feb 2031 comes from the panel framing, not from Marcus's sentence.

evidence.note: HEPI survey of UK undergraduates, fielded Dec 2025. That is before the forecast, so it describes a different period and cannot show fulfilment.

Gallup survey of US K-12 educators, published Oct 2026: 59% used AI in 2025-26, and most users report time savings. This is partial support. It does not establish substantial change in classroom practice or assessment.
Gallup, Feb-Mar 2026: most teachers have no formal AI policy. This limits claims of institutional transformation but does not show AI is peripheral.

reviews.rationale: The contextual deadline (Feb 2031) is after the evaluation date. Post-forecast evidence shows AI is widely used by educators and saves them time, but it does not show substantial change in ordinary teaching or assessment across a broad population, so the early-resolution rule is not met. The strongest finding on assessment change predates the forecast. The forecast is not yet due, and no contradiction is shown.
